In addition to the ARCHES study, Van Dijk et al. (2024) also examined possible hydrogen demand levels at the airport scale, specifically for the Rotterdam The Hague Airport, the third largest airport in the Netherlands with 2.2 million passengers per year. They found that in a case where 40% of turboprops and 20% of turbofans are replaced with H -powered aircraft by 2050, 2 average daily hydrogen demand would amount to 9.1 MTPD in 2050. To add perspective, Los Angeles International Airport has roughly 40 million passengers per year, so even if H -powered 2 aircraft adoption was about 95% lower than the Rotterdam case and assuming similar aircraft types and flight lengths, we could expect similar magnitude of hydrogen demand at Los Angeles in 2050. If airports like Los Angeles require refueling capacity around 8 MTPD in 2050, dispensed costs could be below the reported 2030 cost of $6.80/kg (see Figure 45) with technology learning that occurs between 2030 and 2050. Few other studies provide an in-depth look at hydrogen demand growth over time in the aviation sector. Studies that have provided demand estimates at either a global or country level tend to focus on net-zero scenarios. Net-zero scenarios reported by IATA (Collins 2022); Oesingmann, Grimme, and Scheelhaase (2024); and IEA (2023) estimate direct hydrogen use in airplanes to reach levels between 8 and 20 MMT per year by 2050 at a global scale. BNEF estimates global hydrogen consumption for direct use in aircraft could reach 44 MMT/yr by 2050 in their net-zero case. BNEF also breaks out the U.S. aviation sector direct hydrogen consumption in their net- zero scenario, estimating 9.5 MMT/yr by 2050 (BNEF 2025). Additionally, BNEF reports hydrogen demand under an “economic transition” scenario that considers existing policy and otherwise chooses technologies based on cost-competitiveness (BNEF 2025). Notably, global direct use hydrogen for aviation is reported at 0 MMT/yr each year up to and including 2050 in this scenario, and fossil fuels remain the primary aircraft fuel. This is likely due to a high cost of hydrogen that is uncompetitive with the incumbent jet fuel. It also highlights the necessity of further policy support and advancement in technology, which can spur hydrogen infrastructure deployment and reduce costs, if hydrogen is to become an economically viable option.
